source.title: Effective Skill Unlearning through Intervention and Abstention
source.authors: Yongce Li; Chung-En Sun; T. Weng

record.tranche_reason: The study tests skill-specific activation clustering and an inference-time abstention method, bearing on access blocking, but does not test the listed recovery attacks or reproduce the original unlearning methods.
record.gate_note: The study reports no fine-tuning recovery, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompt-only recovery experiment. The Harry Potter method and other prior methods are cited, not tested. Rows record the key-space clustering analysis and the KSD results reported in Table 2; the main Figure 7 and Figure 8 plots are not numerically legible in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes two training-free, inference-time skill-unlearning methods (Neuron Adjust, Key Space Detection) and reports only their own forget/retain performance against a pruning baseline. It runs no relearning, ablation, quantization or prompting attack, and no analysis of whether an existing method deletes or hides knowledge. It does not test robustness, so it says nothing on whether unlearning resists simple attacks (A) or on any recovery route (B–E). It also makes no robustness claim (F). KSD is an output-abstention filter that leaves the weights unchanged. It is not evidence about other methods being shallow. The Harry Potter method is only cited.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that Neuron Adjust and KSD are lightweight, training-free skill-unlearning methods. They report over 80% relative drop on the target skill and under 10% drop on MMLU and other skills. They say KSD achieves near-perfect unlearning by blocking query vectors from skill-specific key space. They do not examine recovery or robustness.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes training-free, inference-time neuron adjustment and key-space abstention, not gradient ascent, Who's Harry Potter, RMU, or the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Key Space Detection outcomes depend on the hypercube size coefficient alpha; the paper states that alpha is selected to balance forgetting and retained capability.

fits_no_version.finding: Math (GSM8K) and code (MBPP) queries form separable clusters in the last FFL key space of llama-3-8b. The separation holds for alpha 15–20 and degrades above 20. KSD exploits this by refusing output, leaving the knowledge in the weights.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Skill-specific queries cluster in FFL key space, enabling abstention-based skill suppression without weight changes.

fits_no_version.finding: KSD on Llama-3-70B drops GSM8K from 47.5% to 8.1% and MBPP from 61.1% to 0.5% while MMLU stays at 64.8%. This is an inference-time refusal filter's performance with no attack tested.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time abstention filters can suppress targeted skills with negligible MMLU loss.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The experiments run three times and report the best result; no error bars or other uncertainty estimates are given. The text does not state a chance-level reference for the target tasks. The main plots are not numerically legible in the supplied text, and no recovery attack is tested.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 7 reports math/code results across four models and Figure 8 reports language-unlearning results, but their plotted values are not legible in the supplied text; no per-model or per-language numeric rows were extractable. The text gives qualitative summaries of those figures.

untested.parts: No simple attack on the unlearned model. Only the authors' own method's forget/retain scores are given, with no chance-level reference.
No activation-direction ablation. No analysis of whether an unlearning method deletes or blocks knowledge; KSD blocks by design, with weights unchanged.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery attack.
KSD and Neuron Adjust are not claimed or tested to resist any recovery attack.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's version ids (V1/V3) do not map to the versions in play. All rows are the study's own method results or motivating probes, so they are relinked to none. Results are the best of three runs, with no uncertainty reported. Figures 7 and 8 (four models, MLQA languages) are illegible and already declared in rows_left_out. Because KSD only abstains at output, the knowledge plainly remains in the weights. This is relevant context for C but is not a test of it.

versions.untested_parts: It evaluates target-skill performance and MMLU retention for its own methods, but does not test simple recovery attacks or report a chance-level reference.

No activation-direction ablation or direct recovery experiment. KSD is described as inference-time access blocking, but the study does not test whether the blocked knowledge can subsequently be recovered.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual prompting, or in-context recovery experiment.
KSD is proposed as a skill-unlearning method, but the study does not test its resistance to the recovery attacks listed in the claim.

relation.reason: Eldan and Russinovich 2023 (an original) appears only in related work, listed as a fine-tuning-based method. WMDP/RMU are not cited. Nothing in the paper relies on or tests the shallow-unlearning finding.

tranche.reason: The paper proposes its own training-free methods (Neuron Adjust, KSD) and reports only their forget/retain results. It runs no relearning, internal-edit, quantization or prompting attack, makes no robustness claim, and does not analyse any existing method.

source_check.notes: All six rows match the text. Table 2 is Llama-3-70B with KSD forgetting GSM8K and MBPP together. A.2 is headed 'Sequential forgetting', but its text says simultaneous. Section 5 says each experiment was run three times and the best result reported. KSD blocks queries at inference time and leaves the weights unchanged, so these rows test no version.
